heuristics.rule: Complete foundational work before leaving a PM role to found a company
heuristics.action: ...solve value proposition, cash burn estimate, and founding team identification before resigning
heuristics.because: Leaving without these solved means burning personal runway on problems that could have been de-risked while still earning a salary

heuristics.rule: Direct SPM-to-VC is rare; most successful PM-to-VC transitions go through VP/CPO or a founding stint first
heuristics.condition: When a senior PM is targeting VC as a next move...
heuristics.action: ...plan for an intermediate step (VP Product, founding, EIR) rather than applying directly to partner roles
heuristics.because: The career examples that succeeded all included operating leadership or founding experience before VC entry

heuristics.rule: Build pivot optionality before you need it, not after burnout hits
heuristics.condition: When a senior PM is still employed and performing well...
heuristics.action: ...invest in thought leadership, target-domain networking, and advisory roles now
heuristics.because: The best leverage for a pivot comes from a position of strength; burned-out job-seeking signals desperation and narrows options

heuristics.rule: Use a transitional role (EIR, CoS, advisory board) to bridge if a direct pivot is not yet credible
heuristics.condition: When a PM lacks the network or credentials for a direct entry into VC, founding, or C-suite...
heuristics.action: ...pursue a 12–24 month bridge role that provides the missing exposure or signal
heuristics.because: Transitional roles compress the credibility gap without requiring a full leap into an unfamiliar domain

heuristics.rule: EIR roles require demonstrated 0-to-1 product creation, not just scaled-product experience
heuristics.condition: When a PM is evaluating EIR eligibility...
heuristics.action: ...assess whether their track record includes building totally new products from scratch, not just scaling existing ones
heuristics.because: VC firms place EIRs to identify and build new companies; scaled-product experience does not validate this specific capability

heuristics.rule: Publish market teardowns and investment theses publicly to position for VC
heuristics.action: ...write up investment analyses on real companies and distribute them before applying to any firm
heuristics.because: VCs assess analytical thinking and point-of-view credibility; published work demonstrates both in a way a resume cannot

decision_factors.factor: Career altitude at time of pivot
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Most viable pivot paths (VC, EIR, CoS at meaningful companies) require GPM/Director+ level; pivoting earlier limits destination quality
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check whether your current title and scope match the minimum bar cited in job descriptions for target pivot roles

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Roles like EIR and founding require demonstrated ability to build new products from scratch; a scaling-only background disqualifies candidates for these paths
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Audit your portfolio: how many products did you create from nothing vs. inherit and grow?

decision_factors.factor: Existing thought leadership and public presence
decision_factors.why_it_matters: For VC and consulting pivots, public credibility as an opinion-maker accelerates entry; its absence creates a cold-start problem
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Assess whether you have published writing, conference talks, or a newsletter that demonstrates domain expertise to strangers

decision_factors.why_it_matters: First consulting clients come from former colleagues; VC roles come through existing VC relationships; without domain network, timelines extend significantly
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Count how many current VCs, founders, or operators in your target domain you have a genuine relationship with (not just LinkedIn connections)

decision_factors.factor: Tolerance for delayed and uncertain feedback loops
decision_factors.why_it_matters: VC outcomes take years vs. weeks for product metrics; founders operate without the validation loops PMs are trained on
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Reflect on whether you have sustained motivation and judgment confidence in environments where outcome signals are slow or absent

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Consulting takes 12–18 months to replace income; founding involves unpaid or underpaid periods; CoS roles may involve pay cuts
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Calculate how many months of living expenses you have saved and what minimum income you need during a transition period

decision_factors.factor: Specific market thesis or domain expertise
decision_factors.why_it_matters: PM-to-founder requires a specific, defensible thesis about a market gap; generalist product experience alone is insufficient to credibly found a company
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Can you articulate a precise, non-obvious insight about a market that your product experience uniquely positions you to act on?

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Failing at founding at 40+ while trying to return to a large-company PM role creates documented friction; the cost of a failed pivot compounds with age
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Model the re-entry scenario explicitly: if the pivot fails in 3 years, what does your PM job search look like at that age?

decision_factors.why_it_matters: VC is an influence-only relationship with portfolio companies; PMs accustomed to owning decisions must genuinely adapt to an advisory posture
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Assess how comfortable you are with outcomes being determined by founders you advise rather than decisions you make directly

decision_factors.factor: Interest in learning from a specific leader vs. independent operation
decision_factors.why_it_matters: CoS is the right path when the primary motivation is altitude exposure and mentorship from a specific executive; it is the wrong path if the goal is autonomous ownership
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Identify whether you have a specific leader whose decision-making you want to learn from; if not, CoS may not be the right vehicle

hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You permanently give up compensation stability, employer brand credibility, defined scope, and team support — and recovering these requires a successful outcome, which happens roughly 10% of the time
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: PMs who underestimate how much employer brand and structured scope were doing for their sense of competence and market value

hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You move from owning decisions to advising on them; your ability to directly drive outcomes disappears, and feedback on whether your judgment was right takes years to arrive
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: PMs who derive satisfaction from execution and measurable short-term impact rather than pattern recognition over long time horizons

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Taking a Chief of Staff role
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Most CoS roles are time-limited (12–24 months) and not a permanent career track; if you don't have a clear exit plan (VP Product, founding, COO), you may find yourself in a prestigious but transient role with unclear next steps
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: PMs who enter CoS hoping it will organically convert into a permanent senior role rather than treating it as a deliberate bridge

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Waiting until burnout to explore pivots
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The conditions that make pivots viable — strong performance, active network, thought leadership — deteriorate during burnout; by the time you act, your leverage has declined
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: High performers who equate busyness with security and defer career optionality-building until a crisis forces the issue

hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Income replacement takes 12–18 months with high variance; the first clients come from personal network, meaning PMs without a cultivated former-colleague network face a significantly longer cold-start period
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: PMs who changed companies frequently or worked in siloed environments and did not invest in relationship maintenance

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Pursuing EIR as a path to founding
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: EIR qualification implicitly requires 0-to-1 product creation experience; PMs who have only scaled existing products will be screened out even at senior levels
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Senior PMs at large companies whose entire career has been spent on established products with existing user bases

failure_patterns.pattern: Leaving a PM role to found a company before solving value proposition, cash burn, and founding team
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Founders romanticize the leap and underestimate how much faster these questions are answered with employed status, network access, and financial stability intact
failure_patterns.consequence: Personal runway burns on foundational questions that could have been de-risked for free; decisions made under financial pressure are lower quality
warning_signs: You have a general idea or domain interest but no specific, validated market thesis
You haven't identified or had serious conversations with potential co-founders before resigning

failure_patterns.pattern: Attempting a direct SPM-to-VC transition without operating leadership or public thought leadership
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: PMs assume their product skills are sufficient signal; they underestimate that VC firms are assessing judgment about teams, markets, and financial models — not just product instinct
failure_patterns.consequence: Applications are rejected or ignored; time is lost without understanding why; the PM circles back to PM roles without having built the missing credentials
warning_signs: You have no published investment theses or market analyses
You have not networked with current VCs to understand the day-to-day role before applying

failure_patterns.pattern: Taking a CoS role without a defined exit plan
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The prestige and proximity to power of a CoS role obscures the fact that it is time-limited and not a destination; PMs assume tenure will convert into a permanent senior role
failure_patterns.consequence: After 12–24 months, the PM exits without a clear next step and must restart a job search from a role that hiring managers find difficult to categorize
warning_signs: You accepted CoS because it sounded impressive rather than because it connects to a specific next role
You have not mapped out the three standard CoS exit paths (VP Product, founding, COO) and which one you are targeting

failure_patterns.pattern: Deferring pivot preparation until burnout forces the issue
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: High-performing PMs conflate job security with career optionality; they assume strong reviews mean they can act whenever they choose, not recognizing that network and thought leadership decay during neglect
failure_patterns.consequence: When the pivot is finally needed, the PM lacks the network depth, public presence, and advisory relationships that would make the transition credible and fast
warning_signs: You have not published, spoken, or advised externally in the past 12 months
You cannot name five relationships in your target pivot domain that you have actively maintained

diagnostic_questions.question: Does your track record include building products from zero, or primarily scaling existing ones?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person qualifies for EIR roles and has the founding-relevant credibility that VC firms and early-stage companies look for
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: How recently did you do this, and can you articulate the specific decisions that created success from scratch?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Which of your target pivot paths still apply given this gap, and how will you get 0-to-1 experience before making the move?

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you published investment theses, market teardowns, or product analyses publicly?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person has established external credibility as a thought leader, which is a prerequisite for VC and consulting pivots
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What audience have these reached, and have any VCs or founders engaged with them?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: What is preventing you from starting now, while still employed, and how long until you would have a meaningful body of work?

diagnostic_questions.question: Can you name the specific market gap or thesis that makes you want to found a company?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the founding interest is driven by a genuine, defensible insight or by dissatisfaction with the current role — which predicts very different outcomes
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Have you validated this thesis with potential customers, and have you identified who would co-found with you?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The desire to found may be about escaping rather than building; explore whether a different pivot (CoS, EIR, new company PM role) addresses the root cause

diagnostic_questions.question: How comfortable are you with outcome feedback that takes years rather than weeks?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person's motivation and decision-making systems are compatible with VC or founding, where short-term feedback loops are absent
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Can you describe a past experience where you sustained conviction and quality judgment over a long period without external validation?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: VC and founding are likely to be psychologically misaligned; explore pivots with faster feedback (consulting, operator leadership)

diagnostic_questions.question: Is there a specific executive you want to learn from, or do you want a CoS role generically?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether a CoS pursuit is strategically motivated (learn from a specific person, bridge to a defined next role) or status-motivated (proximity to power without a plan)
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Have you mapped what you would learn from this person that you cannot get elsewhere, and what the CoS-to-next-role transition looks like?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: CoS without a specific learning or transition rationale is likely to result in 12–24 months of unclear career positioning

diagnostic_questions.question: How many genuine relationships do you currently have with people in your target pivot domain (VCs, founders, operators)?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person has the network infrastructure for a viable pivot or is starting from zero, which dramatically affects timeline and probability
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Are these relationships warm enough that you could ask for an introduction, a referral, or honest feedback about your fit?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Network-building in the target domain should begin immediately and run in parallel with current role; cold pivots without network take 2–3x longer

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your financial runway if your pivot takes 18 months to generate income?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person can make quality decisions during a transition or will be forced into suboptimal choices by financial pressure
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Have you modeled the minimum income you need vs. the likely income trajectory of your target pivot in its first two years?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The pivot plan needs to either include a bridge (advisory work, part-time consulting) or be delayed until runway is sufficient

industry_realities.common_belief: Senior PMs can move directly into VC at the partner level based on product expertise alone
industry_realities.actual_reality: Most successful PM-to-VC transitions go through VP/CPO level first and often include a founding or operating leadership stint; direct SPM-to-partner transitions are rare and require exceptional network or published thought leadership
industry_realities.implication: PMs targeting VC should plan a multi-step sequence rather than applying directly, and should invest years in building the intermediate credentials

industry_realities.common_belief: Founding a startup is a natural next step for any experienced senior PM
industry_realities.actual_reality: Only ~10% of venture-backed startups reach meaningful scale, and failing at founding at 40+ while trying to return to a large-company PM role creates documented friction
industry_realities.implication: The founding decision requires explicit modeling of the failure scenario — specifically, what your re-entry to PM roles looks like if the company fails in 3–5 years

industry_realities.common_belief: Chief of Staff is a prestigious senior role that can become a permanent career track
industry_realities.actual_reality: Most CoS roles are time-limited (12–24 months) and function as rotational fellowships; the standard exit paths are VP of Product, founding, or COO
industry_realities.implication: Accepting a CoS role without a mapped exit plan risks emerging from it with unclear positioning; treat it as a bridge, not a destination

industry_realities.common_belief: Consulting is an immediate income option for experienced PMs who want to leave corporate
industry_realities.actual_reality: Replacing full-time income through consulting takes 12–18 months with high variance, and first clients almost exclusively come from former colleagues and managers
industry_realities.implication: PMs planning a consulting pivot need to start relationship cultivation and thought leadership while still employed, and must have financial runway to absorb the ramp period

industry_realities.common_belief: Any senior PM can qualify for an EIR role at a VC firm
industry_realities.actual_reality: EIR roles typically require GPM/VP Product+ level with demonstrated experience building totally new products in totally new industries from scratch; PMs who have only scaled existing products are not typically competitive
industry_realities.implication: PMs targeting EIR should audit their 0-to-1 experience honestly and seek to build it before applying

industry_realities.common_belief: The skills that make someone a good PM are sufficient to make someone a good VC
industry_realities.actual_reality: VC requires evaluating team quality, financial models, competitive landscape, and macroeconomic context — not just product judgment; it also requires comfort with an influence-only relationship to portfolio companies rather than direct ownership
industry_realities.implication: PMs considering VC should deliberately develop the non-product dimensions (financial modeling, team assessment, market sizing) and honestly assess whether they can thrive without decision-making authority

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Waits until dissatisfied or burned out, then reactively explores options under pressure
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Builds pivot optionality continuously while employed and performing well, long before the option is needed
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Pivots executed from strength produce better outcomes and faster timelines; pivots executed under duress compress options and signal desperation to the target domain

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Wants to found because they're tired of corporate constraints or inspired by founder culture; cannot articulate a specific market thesis
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Has a specific, defensible insight about a market gap derived from product experience, and has already begun de-risking the hypothesis while employed
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Escape-motivated founding leads to premature exits and underprepared launches; thesis-driven founding produces better-prepared founders with higher survival odds

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Applies to VC roles based on PM experience and expects product skills to speak for themselves
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Publishes market teardowns and investment theses, networks with current VCs to understand the role, and targets intermediate steps (EIR, VP Product) to build missing credentials before applying
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: VCs assess judgment about teams, markets, and financial models — not just product instinct; demonstrating this publicly is the only credible signal for outsiders

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Attracted to CoS because of prestige and proximity to executive power; accepts without mapping exit paths
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Evaluates CoS specifically in terms of what they will learn from a particular leader and which of the three standard exit paths (VP Product, founding, COO) they are targeting
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Without a defined exit plan, CoS tenure produces unclear positioning; treating it as a deliberate bridge produces a clean transition to the intended next role

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Assumes senior PM experience is broadly transferable and underestimates the specific credential gaps (0-to-1 experience, financial modeling, public thought leadership) that pivot roles require
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Audits their own track record honestly against the specific requirements of target pivot roles and identifies the gaps they need to close before making the move
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Overestimating transferability leads to wasted applications, unclear rejections, and years of delayed progress; honest gap assessment enables targeted preparation

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Begins networking in a target pivot domain only after deciding to make the pivot, starting from near-zero relationships
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Maintains and builds relationships in potential pivot domains continuously, so that when a pivot decision is made, the network infrastructure already exists
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Cold pivots without network take 2–3x longer and rely on luck; warm pivots through existing relationships compress timelines and increase quality of opportunities
